title: The Deal Without a Deal — Eddie Would Go
units: Geopolitics · Energy · Middle East · 26 min read
Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb and the geopolitics of a war nobody knows how to end
The Deal Without a Deal

On 17 June, Trump signed the end of the Iran war at Versailles. Five months later, Washington and Tehran are negotiating in Muscat over who administers transit through the Strait the war was meant to liberate. Between those two dates there are two compromised straits instead of one, a Saudi monarchy dragged to the front line, and an open debate about who actually won anything.
20 August 2026 · Geopolitics · Energy · Middle East
"If we win one more battle against the Romans, we shall be utterly ruined."
Pyrrhus of Epirus, after Asculum (279 BC) — Plutarch, Life of Pyrrhus, 21.9
THE ORIGINAL ERROR

Declaring the end of the regime in public as the objective of an air campaign was the error from which almost all the others follow. It created an expectation the chosen instrument could not meet within the promised timeframe. It turned any intermediate result into visible failure. And it handed Tehran the frame of survival-as-victory, which is where a revolutionary regime plays best.

It is worth specifying what that argument does not claim, because stated broadly it would mean nothing. It does not claim that regime change was impossible: there are regimes that fell to sustained economic pressure without a foreign boot on the ground. Nor that not striking would have been free: the nuclear programme was a real problem and no available alternative was good. The error lay not in deciding to strike, but in announcing an objective the chosen force could not deliver.

There is a reading that contradicts all of this, and it is worth putting on the table before going further. Captain Lance Gordon (USN, retired) argues in Small Wars Journal that Washington never bet on an immediate collapse: the campaign would be better understood as deliberate Schelling-style coercion, modelled on the North Korean case —sustained pressure on Kharg Island, gas infrastructure and shipping until the regime concludes that yielding is less risky than resisting. The Stimson Center offers the Iranian mirror image: Tehran is not faltering erratically, it is executing its own strategy of coercive risk to force Washington to pull back. On that reading, this is not a failure but an unresolved war of attrition, and the regime-change rhetoric was psychological pressure, not a broken promise.

There is a reply to that. Coercion is measured by what the counterparty concedes, and five months on Iran has conceded neither the nuclear programme, nor the missiles, nor the inspections, while it has obtained an instrument of rent over Hormuz it did not have before. But it is a live hypothesis, and worth bearing in mind in what follows.
I. THE AUTHORITY IRAN INVENTED

The most revealing fact of the post-war period is in none of the fourteen articles of the Islamabad memorandum. It is in a body Iran created on its own initiative before signing and that no negotiator managed to dismantle: the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, PGSA.

Presented in May as a service providing «real-time updates», it is a de facto maritime customs house: vessels must contact it by email, declare ownership, insurance, crew and cargo, and in many cases pay. Some paid up to two million dollars to cross 34 kilometres of water that until February were free. Ebrahim Azizi, chairman of the Iranian Parliament's National Security Committee, said it without ambiguity: the PGSA would offer «specialised services» in exchange for a fee. J.P. Morgan estimated potential revenue of 70 to 90 billion dollars a year —an investment bank projection, not verified income.

Washington sanctioned the PGSA and threatened secondary sanctions. But several operators reached informal arrangements with Tehran to restore the flow, according to CNN, and most of those payments were made in yuan. The market, between Washington's legal risk and Hormuz's physical risk, chooses to pay.

Gregory Brew, of Eurasia Group, summed up the change: Iran demonstrated that it can close the Strait and keep it closed even under intense bombardment, and nobody can take that away now. It is the exact distance between the JCPOA of 2015 and today: it went from negotiating under sanctions to charging a toll on a geography it always had but has only now learned to monetise.

And in July American diplomacy stopped arguing about whether Iran can charge and began arguing about how the passage is administered. Mediation moved to Muscat: according to Axios, Oman leads with Qatar, Pakistan and Egypt involved, facing Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The Omani proposal, described by CNN, envisages two corridors: the southern one, in Omani waters, with free navigation on pre-war terms; the northern one, in Iranian waters, where permission would have to be requested from Tehran. No tolls.

Iran rejected it and counter-proposed more control of its own, invoking the precedent of the Strait of Malacca, where Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore request voluntary contributions to fund navigation, environmental protection and search and rescue.

One possible interpretation —and it is interpretation, not fact— is that Tehran is not after money, which it already collects, but the legal framework that turns extortion into a tariff. But the analogy has a problem worth naming. The Malacca scheme arises from the Law of the Sea Convention and its regime of transit passage, under which coastal states may neither condition nor tax passage: the contributions work because they are voluntary and decoupled from permission, and nobody is prevented from crossing for failing to contribute. Iran signed that Convention in 1982 and never ratified it, and has maintained ever since that transit passage does not bind it. The PGSA does exactly the opposite of Malacca: it conditions passage on prior authorisation.

There lies the incoherence: Tehran claims the precedent that emanates from a legal framework it rejects, and for a use that framework prohibits. Which does not mean it is of no use to it. In practice, whoever decides whether a vessel crosses is not a court but an underwriter.

The Iranian foreign ministry set out its position without circumlocution —the situation «cannot go back to what it was before the war»— and its declared objective in Muscat is a temporary arrangement of up to three months under which it administers a controlled corridor. What is being negotiated is not an architecture: it is an extension.
Washington went to war, among other reasons, to prevent Iran from controlling Hormuz. Five months later it is discussing the terms of that control.
II. WHO IS IN CHARGE IN TEHRAN?
There is a gap in almost all the coverage, and it is the most important one for knowing whether any agreement can hold: it is not clear who is being negotiated with.

Ali Khamenei was assassinated on 28 February along with much of the security leadership. Trump declared that 48 senior figures died in the bombings, and admitted something revealing: his administration had preferred candidates for the succession, but «the strike was so successful that it eliminated most of the candidates».

On 8 March the Assembly of Experts designated Mojtaba Khamenei, 56, son of the eliminated leader. The IRGC and the armed forces backed him quickly. But American officials maintained that he is injured, and analysts note that he never held an executive office. Ten days later, Ali Larijani —secretary of the Supreme National Security Council and the public face of the war's direction— was also assassinated.

Three consequences run through everything else. Any commitment reached in Muscat is worth whatever the new leadership's capacity to impose it on the IRGC is worth, since the IRGC is what operates the PGSA and the mines. The elimination of the generation that negotiated the JCPOA leaves the ground to younger, harder cadres with no negotiating experience. And a leadership that is weak internally has less room, not more, to concede: it needs external confrontation as a source of authority.

Anyone expecting a technical agreement on navigation to lead to a political one on the nuclear programme is assuming that someone exists in Tehran with the power to sign the second. That premise is not established.
III. LEBANON: THE WAR NOBODY SIGNED

The memorandum says the ceasefire applies «to all fronts, including Lebanon». Israel did not sign it, did not take part in the Switzerland negotiations, and Netanyahu made it known that the fight against Hezbollah «is not over».

The pattern was set early. In April, hours after a two-week pause was announced, fifty Israeli fighters dropped some 160 bombs on a hundred targets in ten minutes. Netanyahu clarified that the truce did not include Lebanon; Pakistan, the mediator itself, maintained the opposite; Trump called Lebanon a «separate skirmish». In June, Hezbollah also rejected the ceasefire Israel and the Lebanese state had agreed: not even the armed actor is bound by what its own state signs.

Trump called Netanyahu in June and the conversation, according to Axios, was described by two officials as loaded with insults, with one unusually blunt line —«you would be in jail if it weren't for me». Netanyahu did not yield: he keeps troops in the «security zones» of southern Lebanon, and his minister Ben-Gvir told him publicly that it was time to say «no» to Trump.

Daniel Shapiro, former ambassador to Israel, described the mechanism: a single Hezbollah rocket over northern Israel is enough for pressure on Netanyahu to spike, which gives Hezbollah —and Iran— considerable control over the dynamic. It was activated on 20 June and has not stopped working since. Tehran does not need to break its agreement with Washington in order to pressure it: it only has to wait for Netanyahu to break his.
IV. KUSHNERISM: FRIEDMAN'S FRAME, NOW LITERAL

Thomas Friedman proposed in The New York Times, on 24 June, the distance between what he calls «Kushnerism» —after Jared Kushner— and «Khomeinism». The first treats geopolitics as a real estate transaction: each side gives something up and the deal is measured in financial gain or loss. The second never played that game: it measures in regime survival and territorial control. Hence the line that made the column circulate: the memorandum «reads like a real estate bankruptcy filing». Friedman quotes the speaker of the Iranian Parliament, Ghalibaf: the agreement is a record of the failure of the United States, and people are going to judge it.

His political thesis is that Trump signed out of electoral calculation: he sold Israel and the Arab states of the Gulf in exchange for Pennsylvania, Georgia and Michigan, because food inflation and the price of petrol were a recipe for losing the midterms. It should be noted that this is a columnist's reading, not that of a source with access to the decision-making process, and that attributing a single motive to a presidential decision simplifies.

What is verifiable is that the frame stopped being a metaphor: Kushner is part, alongside Witkoff, of the delegation in the Omani channel. The same transactional logic now operates against a counterparty that measures in survival.

Friedman had anticipated the dilemma in an interview with CNN: he said he felt torn between wanting to see the Iranian regime militarily defeated and not wanting that defeat to politically strengthen «two terrible human beings», as he described Trump and Netanyahu. It connects with the question the memorandum leaves open: what is the use of winning militarily if the political result is a stronger Trump and Netanyahu and a more unstable region.
V. CHINA: THE BUSINESS OF REPLACING THE GULF
China is the actor that emerged from this war with the most relative power. On that there is consensus. What is badly argued is where it won.

The verifiable part first, which is market data. According to Morgan Stanley and Bloomberg Intelligence cited by CNBC, Beijing cut its crude purchases from 11.7 million barrels a day in February to some 9 million by the end of May —the equivalent of Japan's entire daily consumption. That prevented Brent from breaking through 120 dollars during the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market. It could do so because it entered the war with between 1.3 and 1.4 billion barrels in reserve, more than the 32 countries of the International Energy Agency combined, and because, according to Bruegel, it has maintained since 2021 a 25-year agreement with Iran guaranteeing it crude below market price.

But cutting imports is defence. The offensive position was elsewhere, and Paul Krugman formulated it in April with a headline that admits no nuance: the big winner of the Iran war is Chinese electrotech. The logic is simple. When the price of fossil fuels spikes, the electric alternative becomes irresistible, and the most exposed countries are the ones with the most urgent incentive to accelerate. Sam Butler-Sloss, of Ember, put it better than anyone: fossil prices are, in essence, a geopolitical tax.

The data from the first stretch of the conflict support the thesis. Chinese solar technology exports hit a record in the first month of the crisis. Foreign sales of electric and hybrid vehicles grew 140% year on year. Lithium-ion battery exports rose 50.4% in the first quarter. And behind those numbers there is a structure: China controls more than 80% of world manufacturing capacity for solar panels, wind turbines and batteries.

Ember coined the term in December 2025. China is an «electrostate»: the first major economy where electric technologies became the dominant engine of energy growth. Its diagnosis was blunt —Beijing is not manufacturing clean technology hardware, it is manufacturing an energy future in which it occupies the dominant position.

And there is one figure that reorders everything else: more than 30% of Chinese final energy consumption already comes from electricity, the highest share among the large economies and almost ten points above the United States.

On this picture, Fareed Zakaria published on 17 July —simultaneously in The Washington Post and Foreign Policy— the geopolitical reading of the matter: the greatest beneficiary of the war is China, without firing a shot, without spending enormous sums and without burning political capital. The war would have accelerated three long-standing Chinese objectives: a Middle East less dependent on America, a world more dependent on critical Chinese technology, and a reputation for Beijing as a stable power. It does not seek to replace Washington as the Gulf's military guarantor, which is expensive, but rather for the Gulf to detach partially from the American orbit.
It is correct in direction. But it measures victory in diplomatic influence, and the victory was industrial.

That does not erase Chinese exposure, which remains enormous. The Gulf provides close to half the crude China imports and a third of its liquefied gas, and around 80% of its imports pass through the Strait of Malacca —a dilemma Hu Jintao named in 2003 and that remains unresolved: the Kyaukpyu pipeline has capacity for some 440,000 barrels a day against imports of eleven million.

And there is a detail that shifts the axis of power. What effectively paralysed transit through Hormuz was not Iranian naval power but the insurance market. As Foreign Policy documented in May, war risk premiums jumped from around 0.25% of hull value to between 3% and 10%: for a 250 million dollar tanker, from 625,000 to 7.5 million per voyage, rendering transit commercially unviable. The decision was taken by the Joint War Committee of the Lloyds Market Association, a panel of Western underwriters whose guidance even Chinese insurers follow, and on which Beijing has no representation.

China discovered that its energy supply can be cut off by a regional actor with naval mines, or by a committee of underwriters in London. It controls neither. But it is getting out of oil faster than any other large economy.
There lies the asymmetry the geopolitical reading misses: Chinese vulnerability is real and decreasing; the dependence China generates in others is real and increasing.

Because electrification does not eliminate the geopolitical tax. It changes the recipient. According to Goldman Sachs data, China refines 60% of battery lithium, 65% of nickel and 68% of cobalt, and controls between 85% and 90% of rare earth refining and 92% of magnet manufacturing. The tax moves from the Persian Gulf to Chinese processing plants. A solar panel already installed on a German roof cannot be switched off by Xi Jinping; the lithium that has not yet left the mine can be, as already happened with germanium and gallium.

The most uncomfortable twist is supplied by the Gulf countries themselves. Saudi Arabia was dragged into this war —as of 1 August, American and Saudi aircraft were jointly striking sites in Iraq— and emerged with its export model in crisis. But the way out of that crisis runs through accelerating the energy diversification it had already planned, and the cheapest, most available and most mature technology for doing so is Chinese. The countries whose export collapse caused the global shock end up being one more vector consolidating Beijing's industrial dominance.

Two cracks prevent buying the thesis whole. The electrostate is simultaneously the planet's largest consumer and producer of coal: coal accounts for more than 55% of its electricity generation, and CREA warned in February that China will not meet the targets of its own five-year plan nor the commitments to control the growth of coal consumption. And there is a second-order irony: the manufacture of the chips that make electrification possible depends on helium that leaves via Hormuz. Not even the electrical powers are entirely outside the strait.
The defensible formulation is this: China did not win the Gulf. It won the business of replacing it.

A separate mention for Russia, which usually ends up in a subordinate clause and which won without manufacturing anything. It is the only large exporter beyond the reach of both straits: every dollar of geopolitical premium that Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb add to Brent transfers straight to the coffers of a state at war, without negotiating and without exposing itself. If the criterion is value captured per unit of effort, the winner of this war is not in Beijing.
THE DATA — CHINA

A cut of ~3 million barrels a day and a combined reserve larger than that of the 32 IEA countries together. The Gulf provides ~50% of its imported crude and ~80% passes through Malacca. But more than 30% of its final energy consumption is already electricity —the highest among the large economies— and it controls more than 80% of world manufacturing of panels, turbines and batteries, as well as refining between 60% and 92% of the chain's critical minerals. The reserve figures are third-party estimates: China does not publish them.

VI. BAB EL-MANDEB: THE SECOND STRAIT

On 9 June, the commander of the Quds Force, General Esmail Qaani, warned that an escalation would activate a response from the Axis of Resistance to build a «security belt» from Hormuz to Bab el-Mandeb, as documented by the UN Security Council Report.

On 20 July the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, in retaliation for an attack on Sanaa airport they attributed to Riyadh —although the Saudi-backed Yemeni government claimed responsibility. On the 23rd they attacked two Saudi tankers, the Encelia and the Layla, with ballistic and cruise missiles and drones. Brent crossed 100 dollars: some 101 against 79 a month earlier, close to 30% in thirty days.

The logic is surgical. Since the closure of Hormuz, Riyadh had been diverting exports by pipeline towards the Red Sea via Yanbu. Kpler measures 6.2 million barrels a day through Bab el-Mandeb in the last month, two thirds of them Saudi barrels bypassing the Gulf. Closing that passage does not add a problem: it eliminates the improvised solution to the first one.

It erases the escape valve. When the Red Sea became unsafe in 2024, traffic was diverted to the Cape of Good Hope, adding ten to fourteen days of sailing. With Hormuz also compromised, that alternative ceases to exist for Gulf crude, and Suez admits only smaller vessels.

It drags Saudi Arabia to the front line, which Riyadh spent five months avoiding. As of 1 August, American and Saudi aircraft jointly struck sites in Iraq after pro-Iranian drones were launched towards Saudi territory. The monarchy that handled the war with caution is today a co-belligerent.

It confirms that the model is exportable. Physical control plus collection infrastructure has been replicated at a second node. No bilateral agreement between Washington and Tehran defuses that risk on its own: it would take defusing the entire Axis, an objective no nuclear negotiation contemplates.

And a hypothesis: that forced incorporation could have given Riyadh a veto over Washington's timing. A CNN analysis attributes part of Trump's decision to postpone further strikes to Saudi pressure. It is a single source and explicitly conditional, insufficient to assert a structural change. It is worth keeping as a line of observation.
THE DATA — BAB EL-MANDEB

~6.2 million barrels a day of transit, two thirds of them Saudi barrels redirected after the closure of Hormuz. An effective closure would cut global supply by around 6%, on top of a ~10% fall already caused by Hormuz. Brent from ~79 to ~101 dollars in thirty days.
Kpler · EIA · Al Jazeera · The Hill · The Washington Post
VII. WHY THE MARKET DOES NOT AGREE
There is a contradiction in all of the above, and it is better resolved than dodged.

If the buffers are exhausted and there are two compromised straits, the price should rise. Today the opposite is happening: crude is easing, American equity markets are heading for record highs and the oil majors are posting record profits.

Three explanations, not mutually exclusive. Demand destruction: five months of high prices cool activity, and lower demand needs less supply. Logistical adaptation: rerouting worked better than expected, with routes, insurance and arrangements —including the payments to the PGSA— that official statistics capture poorly. Market disagreement with that assessment of the risk: the dominant expectation appears to be that the Omani channel produces some opening, and if the market is right, the probability of a sustained escalation is overstated.

That third one has to be written down. Markets are not infallible —they underestimated geopolitical risk before February— but nor are they naive, and when analysis and price diverge for weeks, the burden of proof shifts towards the analysis.

There is a fourth reading, and it is the most unsettling: that the adaptation is real and that this is the problem. When the cost of a war stops being felt on the supermarket shelf and at the pump, the main political incentive to end it disappears.
VIII. PHASE ONE, PHASE TWO

The obligatory comparison is the peace plan for Gaza —which entered Phase II in January with a National Committee, a Board of Peace chaired by Trump and a Security Council resolution, and which five months later the Washington Post described as stalled, with donations non-existent, Hamas not disarmed and Israel expanding occupation. Netanyahu himself called those advances «merely declarative».

The Iranian memorandum did not suffer that fate: it did not dilute, it collapsed. Eight days after Islamabad an Iranian drone struck a commercial vessel in Hormuz. On 8 July, in Ankara, Trump declared the ceasefire over and that night the United States hit 90 targets, widening the map as far as the Bushehr area —something that had not happened even in the hardest phase of the original war. On the 14th the naval blockade was reimposed. NPR summed up on the 18th that both countries were staggering towards total war.

And at the beginning of August the phase architecture reappeared, in those words. Trump accused Tehran of duplicity for negotiating while denying it was negotiating, said the talks were under way and projected that Hormuz could open fully as «phase one», with denuclearisation as a «second phase» that would take time. On the other side, the Iranian spokesman Baghaei declared that Iran does not negotiate with Washington, that its negotiators deal with Oman only on the passage of vessels, and that bilateral matters are left for later stages.

Both sides describe the same table in irreconcilable ways: a two-phase peace negotiation against a technical conversation with a third party. It is what Ian Bremmer described before June —each side sells the agreement as a victory and they contradict each other about what was agreed, which leaves abundant ways to derail.

The underlying problem is not rhetorical. Phase I is built on some form of recognition of Iranian control, and Phase II —nuclear, inspections, missiles— is again left suspended on political will instead of enforceable mechanisms. It is the design that already failed this year in Gaza, applied to a state of 81 million inhabitants, with its own army, control of a global passage and a leadership whose capacity to commit nobody can establish.
IX. WHAT REMAINS

There is an optimistic reading that should not be dismissed: there is an active table, mediators with genuine incentives, and a Gulf that needs to stabilise. Bremmer acknowledged it when he said that reopening the Strait takes the most dangerous variable out of the global economy. If Gordon is right and this is coercion in progress, the outcome may yet prove Washington right.

But the complete reading requires holding two ideas together: that any agreement is better than the war, and that none of those attempted resolved a single one of the structural questions the war opened.

Iran built, in the middle of a war, the infrastructure to monetise a global passage, and negotiates its recognition by invoking a precedent that does not fit but that it may not need. Israel demonstrated that it derails on its own any agreement negotiated in its name. The Houthis demonstrated that the model replicates. Saudi Arabia was dragged into a war it did not want. China did not win the Gulf: it won the business of replacing it. Russia collects a rent it did not negotiate. And in Tehran, nobody on the outside can say who has the authority to sign.
Every relevant actor came out with something. The one who started it came out with a table in Muscat where the toll it went to prevent is being discussed.

There the argument from the beginning returns: promising in public a result the chosen instrument could not deliver within the promised timeframe was not a tactical error correctable with more bombing. It was an error about what can be bought with what.
A strait is not conquered: it is administered. And the administration has ended up, for now, on the wrong side of the table.
